text: A distributed service can preserve safety during leader changes by separating the election of a coordinator from the commitment of operations. Each participant records a monotonically increasing term and rejects messages from older terms. A proposed operation becomes committed only after a quorum stores it, and a new coordinator first reconciles its log with a quorum before accepting new operations. Because any two majorities intersect, the reconciliation step exposes at least one copy of every previously committed operation. The coordinator can therefore extend a consistent prefix while discarding uncommitted conflicting suffixes. This design does not guarantee progress during an indefinite network partition, but once communication stabilizes and a single coordinator remains, clients can again complete operations without sacrificing the committed history.

Across three workloads, increasing cache capacity reduced median latency but produced sharply different tail behavior. The read-heavy workload improved at every capacity, while the write-heavy workload stopped improving after the working set fit in memory. Under the mixed workload, the largest cache unexpectedly increased the ninety-ninth percentile because background eviction scans competed with request processing. CPU utilization remained below saturation, and disabling the scans removed most of the regression. These observations suggest that capacity alone is not an adequate tuning objective: maintenance work and its scheduling must be considered when interpreting the apparent benefit of a larger cache.
